newsitem.title: POLAND: Solidarity risks Polish referendum defeat.
newsitem.headline: Solidarity risks Polish referendum defeat.

text.p: Solidarity is leading Poland's rightist opposition into probable defeat in a constitutional referendum on May 25, unafraid that this might reflect badly on its prospects at parliamentary polls due in September.

Solidarity chief Marian Krzaklewski last week urged the trade union's supporters to reject a draft new Polish constitution agreed by the ruling ex-communists, their Peasant coalition partners and two opposition parties in parliament.
Solidarity Election Action (AWS), an alliance grouping dozens of rightist parties around the union, followed suit. @
The outright call for a large turnout against the draft constitution might seem rash, as opinion surveys suggest more Poles are likely to accept than reject it.
Poles have long debated a new constitution, to replace the 1952 Stalin-era one and an interim charter adopted as a stopgap after the fall of communism in 1989.
Solidarity and the right, under-represented in parliament since a rout in 1993 polls, have produced their own version which invokes God and implicitly bans abortion. @
They scorn parliament's often awkward compromise on these and other controversial issues and blame parliament for not letting Poles choose between the two alternatives.
Some analysts see the referendum as a dry run ahead of the September elections.
"The referendum will be largely a political event showing the size of support for extra-parliamentary opposition groups," the public CBOS polling institute said in a report on Friday.
But Solidarity leaders and other analysts argue that a lost referendum, especially if turnout is low, would not necessarily mean an electoral setback for the right in September. @
"It's not a question of losing the referendum. We all stand to lose because this constitution draft is so bad," Czeslaw Bielecki, leader of one of the AWS parties, told reporters.

"This is not a confrontation you can compare with an election in any way," he said, pointing out that there is no minimum turnout below which the vote is invalid and complaining that ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski's office was unfairly campaigning for acceptance of parliament's draft. @

Opinion polls suggest Solidarity is likely to lose the referendum -- for example a survey by the independent Pracownia Badan Spolecznych found that 55 percent of those who intended to vote at all would cast their voices for approving the draft.

PBS said only 13 percent would clearly vote "no" as urged by AWS and the more radical Movement for the Reconstruction of Poland (ROP), while the rest were undecided. It found 56 percent of Poles intended to take part for sure and 21 percent thought they would, while only 14 percent did not plan to vote. @
By contrast, surveys of general election intentions show the AWS rivalling or sometimes outstripping the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) for top place.
A CBOS poll showed on Friday that AWS was leading its SLD foes in mid-April by 26 percent to 23 percent.

Halina Franczak of the independent Demoskop polling agency said she thought the right would fail to stop the parliament's version of the charter but added: "They will not emerge from this badly at all, there is no special risk." @
She told Reuters Poles would vote for the constitution, even though many thought it flawed, because there was a strong desire in society for stability and legislative structures.

But the referendum would allow the right to focus on its broad ideals and values rather than on specific social and economic issues where policy differences with the ruling parties were often hard to convey to voters.
